I. THE PARTIES
A. Defendant Federal Election
Commission
1. Defendant Federal Election
Commission (“FEC” or Commission”) is an
independent agency of the United States with
exclusive jurisdiction over the administration,
interpretation, and civil enforcement of the
Federal Election Campaign Act (“FECA”), 52
U.S.C. § § 30101-46. The Commission is
empowered to formulate policy with respect to
FECA, id. § 30106(b)(1)); to make rules and
regulations necessary to carry out the Act, i d.
§§ 30107(a)(8), 30111(a)(8), 30111(d)); to issue
advisory opinions concerning the application of
FECA and Commission regulations to any
proposed transaction or activity, id. §§ 30107(a)(7),
30108; and to civilly enforce the Act and the
Commission’s regulations, i d. §§ 30106(b)(1);
30109.
B. Plaintiffs
1. National Republican Senatorial
Committee
2. Plaintiff National Republican
Senatorial Committee (“NRSC”) is a national
political party committee of the Republican Party .
(Declaration of Paul Clark (“Clark Decl.”) ¶ 3, FEC
Exh. 13 (Doc. 3-13, PageID 1284).) The purpose of
the NRSC is to “promote the election of Republican
candidates for the United States Senate.”
(RPP_0000174 Articles of Incorporation and
Statement of Conversion of NRSC at 1, FEC Exh.

378

164 (Doc. 40- 4, PageID 3873); see also
RPP_0000178 Bylaws of NRSC, Art. II, FEC Exh.
165 (Doc. 40-5, PageID 3878).)
3. The NRSC is directly governed by
Republican U.S. Senators —its current Chairman
is Senator Steve Daines . About Us, NRSC,
https://www.nrsc.org/about-us/ (last visited Nov. 6,
2023); see also RPP_0000179 Bylaws of the NRSC,
Art. III, FEC Exh. 165 (Doc. 40 -5, PageID 3879).
The Chairman of the NRSC is elected by the
Republican Senate caucus. (RPP_0000180 Bylaws
of NRSC, Art. VI, Section 6.03, FEC Exh.165 (Doc.
40-5, PageID 3880).)
2. National Republican
Congressional Committee
4. Plaintiff National Republican

(Clark Decl. ¶ 3, FEC Exh. 13 (Doc. 36-13, PageID

II. THE FOUNDING ERA AND LATER
AMENDMENTS ESTABLISH THE
PREVENTION OF PARTY -RELATED
CORRUPTION AS A CONSTITUTIONAL
INTEREST OF THE HIGHEST ORDER
AND LEGISLATIVE EFFORTS TO
ADDRESS IT ARE CONSISTENT WITH
THE FOUNDING-ERA UNDERSTANDING
OF THE FIRST AMENDMENT
A. Concerns About Political Party
Corruption Animated the Founding
1. General Corruption Concerns
Predominated the Constitutional
Debates
8. Disenchanted by the rampant
corruption in British government and in the states,
the Framers of the Constitution crafted the
nation’s supreme law with anti -corruption
principles firmly in mind, as demonstrated by the
Constitutional Convention and state r atification
debates, as well as writings at the time. ( See infra
Part II.A.1.)
9. In drafting the Constitution, the
Framers intended to ensure “corruption was more
effectually guarded against, in the manner this
government was constituted, than in any other
that had ever been formed.” 4 Debates in the
Several State Conventions on the Adoption of the
Federal Constitution 302 (Jonathan Elliot ed., 2d
ed. 1836) (Charles Pinckney) (excerpt Jan. 18,
1788) [hereinafter Debates in the State

381

Conventions], FEC Exh. 14 (Doc. 36 -14, PageID
1313).
10. Indeed, “there was near unanimous
agreement [among the delegates at the 1787
Constitutional Convention] that corruption was to
be avoided, that its presence in the political system
produced a degenerative effect, and that the new
Constitution was desig ned in part to insulate the
political system from corruption.”  James D.
Savage, Corruption and Virtue at the
Constitutional Convention , 56 J. Pol. 174, 181
(1994), FEC Exh. 15 (Doc. 36- 15, PageID 1328).
Fifteen of the most important delegates to the
Constitutional Convention, including James
Madison, Gouverneur Morris, George Mason, and
James Wilson use the term corruption no less than
54 times, see id. at 177 (Doc. 36-15, PageID 1324),
and corruption was explicitly identified as a
primary motivator of the Convention . 2 The
Records of the Federal Convention of 1787  288
(Max Farrand ed. 1911) (John Francis Mercer)
(excerpt Aug. 13 -14, 1787) [hereinafter Farrand’s
Records], FEC Exh. 16 (Doc. 36 -16, PageID 1358)
(“What led to the appointment of this Convention?
The corruption & mutability of the Legislative
Councils of the States.”).
11. As Madison wrote in Federalist 51,
“[i]f men were angels, no government would be
necessary. If angels were to govern men, neither
external nor internal controls on government
would be necessary.” The Federalist No. 51, at 337
(Modern Library College eds. 1937), FEC Exh. 17,
(Doc. 36 -17, PageID 1366). As such, avoiding
corruption was critical to structuring a republican

382

government “which derives all its powers directly
or indirectly from the great body of the people . . .
not from . . . a favored class of it.” The Federalist
No. 39, at 243-44 (Madison), FEC Exh. 18 (Doc. 36-
18, PageID 1370-71).
12. The actual and perceived corruption
pervading British politics loomed large over the
Convention and shaped the debates . For example,
the Framers debated at length whether legislators
should be barred from simultaneously holding
other government offices, which was accepted
practice in Great Britain. 1 Farrand’s Records 376
(Pierce Butler) (excerpt June 22 -23, 1787), FEC
Exh. 19 (Doc. 36 -19, PageID 1383) (stating that
“the source of the corruption that ruined [Great
Britain’s] Govt” was that “men got into Parlt[,] that
they might get offices for themselves or their
friends”).
13. It is clear from contemporary sources
that the Framers viewed corruption as an
existential threat . As such, their approach to
corruption was thoroughly prophylactic: “if we do
not provide against corruption our government will
soon be at an end.” Id. at 392 (Mason) (Doc. 36-19,
PageID 1399).
2. The Framers Identified “Faction” -
Related Corruption as Dangerous to
the Nation, Including to Elections
a. The Framers Believed That
Corruption From Faction Would
Harm the Republic
14. The Framers repeatedly singled out
faction, and the corruption risks inherent to it, as

383

harmful to governance and national unity . By
“faction,” the Framers were referring to what are
now called political parties . Richard Hofstadter,
The Idea of a Party System: The Rise of Legitimate
Opposition in the United States, 1780 -1840 10-11
(1970), FEC Exh. 20 (Doc. 36- 20, PageID 1404) .
Explaining the pervasive political beliefs of 18th
century thinkers, the historian Richard Hofstadter
has written, “the root idea we find is that parties
are evil.”  Id. at 9 (Doc. 36- 20, PageID 1403).
15. In the Framers’ conception, “[f]action
and enthusiasm are the instruments by which
popular governments are destroyed.” 2 Debates in
the State Conventions 10 (Fisher Ames) (excerpt
Jan. 15, 1788), FEC Exh. 21 (Doc. 36- 21, PageID
1413). Alexander Hamilton framed the
Constitution’s role in eradicating faction in the
strongest possible terms: “We are attempting, by
this Constitution, to abolish factions, and to unite
all parties for the general welfare.” 2 Debates in the
State Conventions 320 (Hamilton) (ex cerpt June
25, 1788), FEC Exh. 22 (Doc. 36-22, PageID 1437).
As renowned political scientist E. E.
Schattschneider explained:
[T]he authors of the Constitution set up
an elaborate division and balance of
powers within an intricate
governmental structure designed to
make parties ineffective . It was hoped
that the parties would lose and exhaust
themselves in futile attempts to fight
their way through the labyrinthine
framework of the government…. This is
the antiparty part of the constitutional

384

scheme. To quote Madison, the “great
object” of the Constitution was “to
preserve the public good and private
rights against the danger of such a
faction [party] and at the same time to
preserve the spirit and form of popular
government.”
E. E. Schattschneider, Party Government 7 (1942)
(excerpt) (footnote omitted), FEC Exh. 23 (Doc. 36-
23, PageID 1446) (citing The Federalist No. 10 ,
FEC Exh. 24 (Doc. 36-24, PageID 1453)).
b. The Framers Viewed Corruption
and Faction As Perpetuating Each
Other
16. Central to the Framers’ wariness
regarding factions was the recognition, during the
founding era, that faction is a vector by which
external forces may corrupt the government and
that, in turn, corruption itself can cause faction .
Political parties were “conventionally condemned
by political writers” during the 18th century
because, inter alia, they were viewed as potential
agents of corrupt special interests . Hofstadter at
12, FEC Exh. 20 (Doc. 36-20, PageID 1405).
17. By the founding era, it was recognized
that:
[A] party or faction was very likely to
become the instrument with which
some small and narrow special interest
could impose its will upon the whole of
society, and hence to become the agent
of tyranny.

385

Id. (Doc. 36 -20, PageID 1405) . Moreover, by the
mid- and late 1800s, it was clear that corruption
“was the consequence of . . . the existence of
factions.” Savage at 175, FEC Exh. 15 (Doc. 36-15,
PageID 1322).
18. As George Washington underscored
in his farewell address, faction leaves the
government open to corruptive outside forces .
Specifically, he warned that faction:
[S]erves always to distract the public
councils, and enfeeble the public
administration. It agitates the
community with ill -founded jealousies
and false alarms ; kindles the animosity
of one part against another ; foments
occasionally riot and insurrection . It
opens the door to foreign influence and
corruption, which finds a facilitated
access to the government itself, through
the channels of party passions.
George Washington, Farewell Address to the
People of the U.S. of America 8 (A. Boyd Hamilton
publ. Sept. 17, 1797), FEC Exh. 25 (Doc. 36 -25,
PageID 1464) (emphasis added); see also  The
Federalist No. 68, at 442 (Hamilton), FEC Exh. 26
(Doc. 36-26, PageID 1475) (explaining that “cabal,
intrigue, and corruption” should be expected “to
make their approaches from more than one
quarter, but chiefly from the desire in foreign
powers to gain an improper ascenda nt in our
councils”).
19. Simultaneously, the Framers
understood that corruption stokes faction .

386

Benjamin Franklin expressed deep fears about the
success of the American experiment, stating that:
The struggles for [money and power] are
the true sources of all those factions
which are perpetually dividing the
Nation, distracting its councils, hurrying
sometimes into fruitless & mischievous
wars, and often compelling a submission
to dishonorable terms of peace.
1 Farrand’s Records  82 (excerpt June 2, 1787),
FEC Exh. 27 (Doc. 36-27, PageID 1484).
c. Elections are Susceptible to
Corruption Enabled by Faction
20. The Framers viewed elections as
vulnerable to corruptive forces, often enabled by
faction, and were cognizant that elected legislators
were vulnerable to corruption . As Hamilton
articulated:
In republics, persons elevated from the
mass of the community, by the suffrages
of their fellow -citizens, to stations of
great pre-eminence and power, may find
compensations for betraying their trust,
which to any but minds animated and
guided by superior virtue, may appear to
exceed the proportion of interest they
have in the common stock, and to over -
balance the obligations of duty.
The Federalist No. 22 , at 138, FEC Exh. 28 (Doc.
36-28, PageID 1500).
21. The Framers were familiar with and
wary of voting corruption at the earliest stages of

387

the democracy. For example, The Boston Gazette,
and the Country Journal published an article on
January 21, 1788, regarding “Bribery and
Corruption!!!,” reporting that:
The most diabolical plan is on foot to
corrupt the members of the Convention,
who oppose the adoption of the new
Constitution. Large sums of money have
been brought from a neighboring state
for that purposes, contributed by the
wealthy. If so, is it not probable there
may be collections for the same accursed
purpose nearer home ? CENTINEL.
2 Debates in the State Conventions 51 (excerpt Jan.
21, 1788), FEC Exh. 29, (Doc. 36-29, PageID 1506)
(quoting the Boston Gazette & the Country
Journal). The article worried those debating
ratification sufficiently that they resolved to “take
measures for inquiring into the subject of the said
publication, and for ascertaining the truth or
falsehood of the suggestion therein contained.”  Id.
(Doc. 36-29, PageID 1506).
22. The Framers were particularly
anxious that factions could influence elections and
introduce regulations “as would render the rights
of the people insecure and of little value.”   2
Debates in the State Conventions 27 (Theophilus
Parsons) (excerpt Jan. 16, 1788), FEC Exh. 30
(Doc. 36 -30, PageID 1526) . In debating a
citizenship requirement for candidacy, the
Framers recognized that, without such a
requirement, “[r]ich men of neighbouring States,
may employ with success the means of corruption

388

in some particular district and thereby get into the
public Councils after having failed in their own
State.”  2 Farrand’s Records 218 (Mason) (excerpt
Aug. 8, 1787), FEC Exh. 44 (Doc. 37 -4, PageID
1813).
23. The appropriate tool to curb faction,
and its attendant corruption, was deemed to be
legislation. Indeed, in Madison’s view, this was an
essential legislative function . He wrote in  The
Federalist that “[t]he regulation of these various
and interfering interests forms the principal task
of modern legislation, and involves the spirit of
party and faction in the necessary and ordinary
operations of government.”  The Federalist No. 10,
at 56, FEC Exh. 24 (Doc. 36-24, PageID 1452).
B. The Text of the Constitution
Addresses Corruption and Faction
24. The Framers’ concerns about
corruption, faction, and the relationship between
them is reflected in the text of the Constitution,
which demonstrates a firm commitment to
employing prophylactic rules to support civil
society and elevate the public good . There was
intensive discussion regarding how various
provisions could best disrupt tendencies toward
faction, many of which were ultimately reflected in
the text . See The Federalist No. 81 , at 525
(Hamilton), FEC Exh. 45 (Doc. 37-5, PageID 1842)
(decrying the “pestilential breath of faction” that
would inhere to a legislature imbued with judicial
powers); The Federalist No. 73 , at 476- 77
(Hamilton), FEC Exh. 46 (Doc. 37-6, PageID 1850)
(explaining that the presidential veto would deter

389

faction in the legislature) . As set forth below,
numerous Constitutional provisions were drafted
to address the issues of corruption and faction head
on.
1. The Foreign Emoluments Clause
25. The Foreign Emoluments Clause
provides that “no Person holding any Office of
Profit or Trust under [the United States], shall,
without the Consent of the Congress, accept of any
present, Emolument, Office, or Title, of any kind
whatever, from any King, Prince, or foreign State.”
U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 8. In a rare show of unity
by the delegates, the Foreign Emoluments Clause
was added to the draft without dissent. 2 Farrand’s
Records 389 (excerpt Aug. 23, 1787), FEC Exh. 47
(Doc. 37-7, PageID 1863). It is one of few portions
of the Constitution imported wholesale from the
Articles of Confederation. Compare U.S. Const. art.
I § 9, cl. 8, with  Articles of Confederation of 1781,
art. VI, para. 1  (“[N]or shall any person holding
any office of profit or trust under the united states,
or any of them, accept of any present, emolument,
office, or title of any kind whatever, from any king,
prince, or foreign state[.]”). It has been understood
to be “‘di rected against every kind of influence by
foreign governments upon officers of the United
States’ . . . in the absence of consent by Congress.”
Application of Emoluments Clause to Part -Time
Consultant for the Nuclear Regul. Comm’n, 10 Op.
O.L.C. 96, 98 (1986), FEC Exh. 48 (Doc. 37 -8,
PageID 1873) (quoting Gifts from Foreign Prince—
Officer—Const. Prohibition, 24 Op. Att’y Gen. 116,
117 (1902), FEC Exh. 49, (Doc. 37- 9, PageID
1878)).

390

26. The Clause was “provided to prevent
corruption” after several high -profile examples of
foreign governments arguably currying favor with
American representatives. See Debates and Other
Proceedings of the Convention of Virginia 330 (2d
ed. 1805) (Edmund Randolph) (excerpt June 17th,
1788), FEC Exh. 50 (Doc. 37-10, PageID 1890). An
infamous example was Louis XVI’s gift of a
bejeweled snuff box to then-ambassador to France,
Benjamin Franklin, which the Framers viewed
with deep suspicion . Id. at 330- 31 (Doc.  37-10,
PageID 1890-91).
27. The Framers were united in their
view that corruption by outside forces posed a real
and present danger to the republic. See 1 Farrand’s
Records 289 (Hamilton) (excerpt June 18, 1787),
FEC Exh. 51 (Doc. 37-11, PageID 1916) (recording
concerns that “one of the weak sides of Republics
[is] their being liable to foreign influence &
corruption” and “[m]en of little character,
acquiring great power become easily the tools of
intermedling neibours”); 2 Farrand’s Records 268
(Elbridge Gerry) (excerpt Aug. 13 -14, 1787), FEC
Exh. 16 (Doc. 36 -16, PageID 1338) (warning that
“[f]oreign powers will intermeddle in our affairs,
and spare no expence to  influence them”); see also
2 Farrand’s Records 389 (Pinckney) (excerpt Aug.
23, 1787), FEC Exh. 47 (Doc. 37- 7, PageID 1863)
(urging “the necessity of preserving foreign
Ministers & other officers of the U.S. independent
of external influence”).
28. The text is not only concerned with
corruption but with its appearance —indeed, it
does permit gifts if  Congress approves them,

391

indicating that the perception of corruption could
be allayed and so render the gift acceptable . See
U.S. Const. art. I § 9, cl. 8.
2. The Domestic Emoluments
Clause
29. Addressing presidential
remuneration, the Constitution states that “[t]he
President shall, at stated Times, receive for his
Services, a Compensation, which shall neither be
encreased nor diminished during the Period for
which he shall have been elected, and he shall not
receive within that Period any other Emolument
from the United States, or any of them.”  U.S.
Const. art. II, § 1, cl. 7.
30. Hamilton captured succinctly the
danger of the type of corruption addressed by the
Domestic Emoluments Clause: that placing the
power to change the president’s salary during his
tenure into the hands of Congress would “render
him . . . obsequious to th eir will . . . either
reduc[ing] him by famine, or tempt[ing] him by
largesses, to surrender at discretion his judgment
to their inclinations.”  The Federalist No.  73, at
474-75, FEC Exh. 46 (Doc. 37 -6, PageID 1849).
Concerns that the executive could be corrupted by
a congress controlling his remuneration were not
abstract nor were concerns that the executive, in
turn, could exploit his post for monetary gain . In
colonies that operated as proprietorships, for
example, “public revenue of the colony belonged to
the private proprietor,” who often was the
governor. Alvin Rabushka, The Colonial Roots of
American Taxation, 1607-1700, Hoover Institution

392

Pol. Rev. at *12 (Aug. 1, 2002), FEC Exh. 52 (Doc.
37-12, PageID 1951).
3. The Ineligibility Clause
31. Pursuant to the Ineligibility Clause,
“[n]o Senator or Representative shall, during the
Time for which he was elected, be appointed to any
civil Office under the Authority of the United
States, which shall have been created, or the
Emoluments whereof s hall have been encreased
during such time.”  U.S. Const. art. I, § 6, cl. 2. The
text is meant to safeguard against legislators
joining Congress to obtain offices . 1 Farrand’s
Records 376 (Butler) (excerpt June 22- 23, 1787),
FEC Exh. 19 (Doc. 36-19, PageID 1383).
32. This Clause serves an interrelated
purpose with the Foreign and Domestic
Emoluments Clauses: preventing temptation of
elected officials, which could lead to actual or
apparent corruption . As Edward Rutledge
explained, the Clause was intended to “preserv[e]
the Legislature as pure as possible, by shutting the
door against appointments of its own members to
offices, which was one source of corruption.”  Id. at
386 (Doc. 36-19, PageID 1393).
33. The corruption of Parliament
members by the crown by way of plumb
appointments served as the inspiration for the
inclusion of the Ineligibility Clause . See id. at 376
(Butler) (Doc. 36-19, PageID 1383). In the Framers’
view, this particular type of corruption “ruined” the
British government . See id. (Doc. 36 -19, PageID
1383). The Clause was viewed as a critical tool
stem the “venality and abuses” of this type

393

rampant in Great Britain at the time . See id.
(Mason) (Doc. 36-19, PageID 1383).
4. Size of the Legislature
34. Article I, Section 2 is the
constitutional mandate for a large House of
Representatives calculated proportionate to the
population of each state. Requiring a larger
number of representatives was designed to stymie
the partisanship that breeds corruption . See 2
Farrand’s Records 66 (Madison) (excerpt July 20,
1787), FEC Exh. 53 (Doc. 37- 13, PageID  1971)
(explaining that “the difficulty of acting in concert
for purposes of corruption was a security to the
public” because “if one or a few members only
should be seduced, the soundness of the remaining
members, would maintain the integrity and
fidelity of the body”).
35. The importance of a large House of
Representatives in particular was viewed as a
necessary check against the smaller senate and the
presidency. “The larger the number,” stated
Elbridge Gerry, “the less the danger of [the House]
being corrupted.”  1 Farrand’s Records 569 (excerpt
July 10, 1787), FEC Exh. 54 (Doc. 37- 14, PageID
1983). The smaller senate was seen, in contrast, as
more easily corruptible . 2 Farrand’s Records 319
(Gerry) (excerpt Aug. 17, 1787), FEC Exh. 55 (Doc.
37-15, PageID 1997) (explaining, when considering
the power of Congress to declare war, that “[t]he
Senate are more liable to be corrupted by an
Enemy than the whole Legislature”); see id. at 279
(Randolph) (excerpt Aug. 13 -14, 1787), FEC Exh.
16 (Doc. 36-16, PageID 1349) (“The Senate will be

394

more likely to be corrupt than the H. of Reps and
should therefore have less to do with money
matters.”).
5. The Veto Power
36. Article I, Section 7, Clause 2 gives the
President the authority to veto a bill, subject to a
veto being overruled by two- thirds of the House
and Senate. U.S. Const. art. I, § 7, cl. 2 . The veto
power provides the most integral check on the
legislature in the finely tuned separation of powers
enacted by the Constitution . Every check of a
branch’s power in the Constitution is responsive to
the fear that it might be possible to “purchase the
guardians of the people.” See The Federalist No. 55,
at 364 (Madison), FEC Exh. 56 (Doc. 37-16, PageID
2003).
37. As Madison explained:
The improbability of such a mercenary
and perfidious combination of the
several members of government
standing on as different foundations as
republican principles will well admit,
and at the same time accountable to the
society over which they are placed,
ought alone to quiet this apprehension.
Id. (Doc. 37-16, PageID 2003).
38. The discussion surrounding the veto
power demonstrates the Framers’ understanding
that checks serve to inoculate against corruption—
and in particular against the corruption attendant
to factions in Congress . Hamilton described the
veto as establishing a “salutary check upon the
legislative body, calculated to guard the

395

community against the effects of faction,
precipitancy, or of any impulse unfriendly to the
public good, which may happen to influence a
majority of that body.” The Federalist No. 73 , at
477, FEC Exh. 46 (Doc. 37-6, PageID 1850).
6. The Elections Clause
39. To enable Congress to regulate
elections, the Constitution states that “[t]he Times,
Places and Manner of holding Elections for
Senators and Representatives, shall be prescribed
in each State by the Legislature thereof; but the
Congress may at any time  by Law make or alter
such Regulations, except as to the Places of
chusing Senators.”  U.S. Const. art. I, § 4, cl. 1.
40. The Elections Clause was included “to
prevent corruption or undue influence” by
ensuring “uniform . . . elections held on the same
day throughout the United States[.]”  2 Debates in
the State Conventions  535 (Thomas M’Kean)
(excerpt Dec. 11, 1787), FEC Exh. 57 (Doc. 37- 17,
PageID 2046). These time and place safeguards
were intended to ensure that Congress was
answerable directly to the people, rather than to
factions that might aim to “mould their regulations
as to favor the candidates they wished to succeed.”
2 Farrand’s Records 241 (Madison) (excerpt Aug.
8-9, 1787), FEC Exh. 44 (Doc. 37- 4, PageID 1836);
see also 1 Farrand’s Records 159 (John Dickinson)
(excerpt June 7, 1787), FEC Exh. 58 (Doc. 37- 18,
PageID 2066) (positing as a primary concern for
electing senators “how . . . you prevent fraudulent
or corrupt Elections”).

396

41. It was also designed to safeguard
against politicians and factions engineering
electoral rules to ensconce themselves or privilege
their interests over those of their constituents. The
Framers’ concern in leaving election regulations
completely in state control was that “when faction
and party spirit run high,” a legislature might take
harmful actions, including “mak[ing] an unequal
and partial division of the states into districts f or
the election of representatives [or] disqualify . . .
electors.” 2 D ebates in the State Conventions 27
(Parsons) (excerpt Jan. 15-16, 1788), FEC Exh. 30
(Doc. 36 -30, PageID 1526); see also  1 Farrand’s
Records 154 (Madison) (excerpt June 7, 1787), FEC
Ex. 58 (Doc. 37 -18, PageID 2061) (arguing that
senators should not be elected by state legislatures
“[i]f an election by the people, or thro’ any other
channel than the State Legislatures promised as
uncorrupt & impartial a preference of merit”).
42. Elections also served a further
security against intra -government corruption: by
varying term lengths, the potential for corruption
of one branch by another was disrupted. See The
Federalist No. 41 , at 265 (Madison), FEC Exh. 59
(Doc. 37 -19, PageID 2073) (drawing attention to
the faults in the British system and its practice of
electing Members of Parliament every seven years,
where “the electors are so corrupted by the
representatives, and the representatives so
corrupted by the Crown”).
7. Constitutional Amendments
43. Concerns regarding corruption
continued to shape the Constitution far beyond the

397

document inked in 1787 . These concerns also
guided the drafting of subsequent amendments at
later points in American history and into the
contemporary era. Enumerated below are several
amendments reflecting the government’s
consistent, persistent concern with cabining
corruption.
a. The First Amendment
44. The First Amendment, in addition to
protecting freedom of speech and the press, also
safeguards the rights of the people “to petition the
Government for a redress of grievances.”   U.S.
Const. amend. 1.
45. The Framers would have understood
the Petition Power as a tool for preventing and
remedying corruption . Its inclusion signaled the
continuation of the long tradition of petitioning in
the colonies and Great Britain, as well as the
intention to embed in the fabric of the government
an obligation to address petitions, which “often
disclose and consequently rem edy incompetence,
corruption, waste, and other government
misconduct.”  Norman B. Smith, “Shall Make No
Law Abridging . . . :”: An Analysis of the Neglected,
but Nearly Absolute, Right of Petition, 54 U. Cin. L.
Rev. 1153, 1178 (1986), FEC Exh. 60 (Doc. 37 -20,
PageID 2087).
b. The Seventeenth Amendment
46. The Seventeenth Amendment
provides that “[t]he Senate of the United States
shall be composed of two Senators from each State,
elected by the people thereof, for six years[.]”  U.S.
Const. amend. 17. This amendment was a natural

398

outgrowth of the Framers’ fear of the potential for
corruption in the small senate body . See, e.g., 2
Farrand’s 319 (Gerry) (excerpt Aug. 17, 1787), FEC
Exh. 55 (Doc. 37-15, PageID 1997).
47. The Framers’ fears about the Senate’s
peculiar vulnerability to corruption were borne out
in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when
Senate elections by state legislatures were rocked
by election corruption scandals. Between 1866 and
1900, nine Senate investigations were called to
review allegations of corruption in Senate election
cases. Ralph A.  Rossum, The Irony of
Constitutional Democracy: Federalism, the
Supreme Court, and the Seventeenth Amendment ,
36 San Diego L. Rev. 671, 707 (1999), FEC Exh. 61,
(Doc. 37-21, PageID 2124).
48. Senator William A. Clark of Montana
was forced to resign in 1899 after confessing to
giving $140,000 to Montana state legislators . Id.
(Doc. 37 -21, PageID 2124) . In 1912, Senator
William Lorimer of Illinois was expelled from the
Senate following reports that four state legislators
were bribed to secure their votes . Id. (Doc. 37-21,
PageID 2124).
49. In drafting the Seventeenth
Amendment, lawmakers were not only concerned
about senators bribing state legislators for
personal advancement. They were also concerned
with the corruption of the Senate by corporate
interests. See Senator Joseph L. Bristow, The
Direct Election of Senators 4-5 (1912), FEC Exh. 62
(Doc. 37 -22, PageID 2170- 71) (asserting that
corporations behaved in a “most reprehensible and

399

scandalous manner” and had spent “enormous
amounts of money in corrupting legislatures to
elect to the Senate men of their own choosing”). As
a result of the demonstrable danger of corruption,
the drafters of the Seventeenth Amendment
endeavored to restructure the election of the
legislative branch, further baking the anti -
corruption principle into the Constitution.
c. The Twenty-Seventh Amendment
50. In 1992, with the belated ratification
of the Twenty-Seventh Amendment, an additional
piece of the Framers’ plan to guard against
corruption through the Constitution fell into place.
The Twenty -Seventh Amendment provides that
“[n]o law, varying the compensation for the
services of the Senators and Representatives, shall
take effect, until an election of Representatives
shall have intervened.”  U.S. Const. amend. 27.
51. A corollary to the Domestic
Emoluments Clause, the amendment, which was
proposed and approved in the 1700s, but not
ratified for another two centuries, was also
responsive to the Framers’ fear of “the apparent
and real corruption of the British constit ution.”
See Richard B. Bernstein, The Sleeper Wakes: The
History and Legacy of the Twenty -Seventh
Amendment, 61 Fordham L. Rev. 497, 501- 02
(1992), FEC Exh. 63 (Doc. 37- 23, PageID 2179)
(tracing the history of the Twenty -Seventh
Amendment).
C. Founding-Era Thinkers Viewed
Legislative Efforts to Promote the
Public Good as Valid, Including

400

Through Laws Impacting Speech
Rights
1. Political Theorists in the
Framers’ Time Viewed Speech as
Subject to Regulation for the
Public Good
52. The political leaders of the founding
era understood that legislation was a legitimate
vehicle by which the public good could be
advanced, even if civil rights, including speech
rights, were impacted. See Jud Campbell, Natural
Rights and the First Amendment , 127 Yale L.J.
246, 313- 14 (2017), FEC Exh. 64 (Doc. 37- 24,
PageID 2249-50).
53. Promotion of the public good was the
primary consideration and basis for evaluating
laws touching on civil rights . As demonstrated in
Nathaniel Chipman’s writings, founding -era
thinkers believed that the exercise of retained
natural rights, such as speech rights, “must be in a
just compromise with the convenience and
happiness of others, agreeably to the laws of social
nature, and such combinations and regulations, as
are clearly derived from those laws.”  Nathaniel
Chipman, Sketches of the Principles of Government
174-75 (1793) (excerpt), FEC Exh. 65 (Doc. 37- 25,
PageID 2301-02); see also The Federalist No. 43, at
287 (Madison), FEC Exh. 66 (Doc. 37- 26, PageID
2310) (“[T]he safety and happiness of society are
the objects at which all political institutions aim.”).
54. Along similar lines, Joseph Priestley
explained that regulation impacting civil liberties
was permissible in order for citizens to operate in

401

a society “for their mutual advantage.”  Joseph
Priestley, An Essay on the First Principles of
Government, and on the Nature of Political, Civil,
and Religious Liberty 12-13 (2d ed.1771) (excerpt),
FEC Exh. 67 (Doc. 37 -27, PageID 2313- 14). In
detailing the basis of state powers, he stated that
the “good and happiness of the members, that is
the majority of the members of any state, is the
great standard by which every thing relating to
that state must finally be determined.”  Id. at 13
(Doc. 37 -27, PageID 2313) . Respecting civil
liberties, he elaborated that “the happiness of the
whole community is the ultimate end of the
government” and claims of individuals at odds with
certain public needs would be required to yield. Id.
at 57 (Doc. 37-27, PageID 2316).
55. It was generally recognized, as
influential jurist Alexander Addison explained,
that speech protections were qualified at the time.
Alexander Addison, Analysis of the Report of the
Committee of the Virginia Assembly on the
Proceedings of Sundry of the Other States in
Answer to Their Resolutions 42 (1800) (excerpt),
FEC Exh. 68 (Doc. 37 -28, PageID 2320); see also
Chipman at 152, FEC Exh. 65 (Doc. 37-25, PageID
2298) (explaining the view that restraints were
permissible where necessary on press freedom and
“public or private discussion”).
56. Consequently, the political leaders in
the founding era viewed limitations on harmful
speech as permissible including, in Addison’s view,
when an individual would “pervert the judgment of
the people, and render it impossible for them to
make a right ch oice” in situations “where the

402

people have a right to choose their magistrates.”
Addison at 42, FEC Exh. 68 (Doc. 37- 28, PageID
2320). Other jurists at the time believed the
common law itself recognized “checks upon
words . . . dangerous to the public welfare.”  See
People v. Ruggles, 8 Johns. 290, 296, 1811 WL 1329
(N.Y. Sup. Ct. 1811), FEC Exh. 69 (Doc. 37 -29,
PageID 2325).
57. Consistent with these principles,
regulations impacting speech based on the public
good were common, and there existed a litany of
laws impacting speech to some degree. See 8
Annals of Congress 2148 -49 (1798), FEC Exh. 70
(Doc. 37 -30, PageID 2328- 29) (detailing various
speech regulations).
58. As set forth above, the Framers
considered disrupting faction and countering its
attendant corruption critical public goods; they
were widely discussed at the Constitutional
Convention and served as the impetus for
numerous constitutional provisions . (See supra
Part II.A-B.)
2. Founding-Era Courts Generally
Did
Not Overturn Important
Regulations of Speech
a. Laws Impacting Civil Rights for
the Public Good Were Generally
Not Struck Down
59. Passing regulations to promote the
public good, even where civil rights including
speech rights were impacted, was widely
considered permissible and not struck down by

403

courts. During the founding era and throughout
the 19 th century, there was “very little room for
judicial oversight” of legislative regulations of
speech designed to serve the common good .
Campbell, Natural Rights and the First
Amendment, at 316, FEC Exh. 64 (Doc. 37- 24,
PageID 2250).
60. The Founders “preserved retained
natural rights principally through constitutional
structure,” and understood legislators to be
empowered to influence the appropriate scope of
those rights . Jud Campbell, Republicanism and
Natural Rights at the Founding , 32 Const.
Comment. 85, 104 (2017), FEC Exh. 71 (Doc. 37-
31, PageID 2336-37).
61. Madison believed that courts’
“latitude in expounding the Constitution” should
be limited to avoid “break[ing] down the
landmarks intended by a specification of the
Powers of Congress” and blurring the separation of
powers. See Letter of James Madison to Spencer
Roane (Sept. 2, 1819), in  8 The Writings of James
Madison 1808-1819 448 (Gaillard Hunt ed., 1908),
FEC Exh. 72 (Doc. 37 -32, PageID 2354) . In his
view, matters of “mere expediency or policy” were
“evidently beyond the reach of Judicial cognizance”
and firmly in the hands of the legislative branch .
Id. at 449 (Doc. 37 -32, PageID 2355); see also
Commonwealth v. Caton , 8 Va. 5, 17 (1782), FEC
Exh. 73 (Doc. 37-33, PageID 2366) (“[H]ow far this
court . . . shall have power to declare the nullity of
a law passed . . . by the legislative power, without
exercising the power of that branch” is a “deep,
important, and . . . tremendous question.”).

404

62. Consistent with the Framers’ view,
founding-era judges repeatedly explained that
judicial review should be limited to “plain and
clear” cases of constitutional violations to avoid the
“danger of the judiciary preventing the operation
of laws which migh t be productive of much public
good.”  E.g., Kamper v. Hawkins, 3 Va. 20, 61 (Va.
Gen. Ct. 1793), FEC Exh. 74 (Doc. 37 -34, PageID
2382); see James B. Thayer, The Origin and Scope
of the American Doctrine of Constitutional Law , 7
Harv. L. Rev. 129, 140 -44 (1893), FEC Exh. 75
(Doc. 37 -35, PageID 2400- 02) (providing an
overview of early approaches to the scope of
judicial review).
63. In Calder v. Bull, the Supreme Court
explained the prevailing view at the time that
though laws may be declared unconstitutional, the
power to do so was of a “delicate and awful nature”
to which the Court “will never resort . . . . but in a
clear and urgent case.”  3 U.S. 386, 399, 1 L. Ed.
648 (1798), FEC Exh. 76 (Doc. 37- 36, PageID
2421). The Court continued that “[i]f . . . the
Legislature . . . shall pass a law, within the general
scope of their constitutional power, the Court
cannot pronounce it to  be void, merely because it
is, in their judgment, contrary to the principles of
natural judgment.”  Id. (Doc. 37-36, PageID 2421);
see also  Ware v. Hylton , 3 U.S. 199, 237 (1796),
FEC Exh. 77 (Doc. 37-37, PageID 2443) (explaining
the contemporaneous view that laws should not be
judged unconstitutional, assuming courts had that
power, except in a “very clear case”).
64. An opinion from a Georgia court
summarizes the approach to judicial review in the

405

era shortly after the First Amendment was
adopted:
[N]o nice doctrines, no critical exposition
of words, no abstract rules of
interpretation, such as may fit the
elucidation of principles in a legal
contest between individuals, can or
rather ought to be resorted to in deciding
on the constitutional operati on of a
statute. The violation of a constitutional
right ought to be as obvious to the
comprehension of every one as an
axiomatic truth: as that the parts are
equal to the whole.
Grimball v. Ross, 2 Am. L.J. 93, 96 (Ga. Super. Ct.
1808), FEC Exh. 78 (Doc. 37-38, PageID 2475).
b. Courts Routinely Enforced Laws
Impacting Speech
65. In accordance with the limited view of
Constitutional review in the founding era, courts
repeatedly enforced laws that impacted speech,
including criminal libel laws. Justice James Iredell
explained the view that “[e]very freeman has an
undoubted right to lay what sentiments he pleases
before the public; to forbid this, is to destroy the
freedom of the press,” but for illegal publications,
“he must take the consequence of his own
temerity.” Charge to the Grand Jury, Case of Fries,
9 Fed. Cas. 829 (C.C.D. Pa. 1799) (Iredell, J.), in 3
The Documentary History of the Supreme Court of
the United States, 1789 -1800 347 (Maeva Marcus
et al. eds., 1990), FEC Exh. 79 (Doc. 37-39, PageID
2497). As a result, his opinion at the time

406

concluded, “the freedom of the press does not
require that libellers shall be protected from
punishment.” Id. at 348 (Doc. 37-39, PageID 2498).
66. Reflecting this sentiment at the time,
there were numerous cases enforcing convictions
for criminal libel . See generally, e.g., People v.
Croswell, 3 Johns. Cas. 337, 1804 WL 874 (N.Y.
Sup. Ct. 1804), FEC Exh. 80 (Doc. 37 -40, PageID
2503-32) (allowing the conviction for criminal libel
to stand pursuant to judge deadlock); Respublica v.
Cobbett, 3 U.S.  467, 475-76 (Pa. 1798), FEC Exh.
81 (Doc. 38 -1, PageID 2550- 51) (finding that
defendant forfeited his good behavior bond for
libelous statements made while awaiting action by
the grand jury).
III. POLITICAL PARTIES HAVE
CONSISTENTLY BEEN INVOLVED IN
ACTUAL AND APPARENT QUID PRO
QUO EXCHANGES, INCLUDING MANY
OF THE NATION’S BIGGEST SCANDALS
AND PARTICULARLY IN CONNECTION
WITH CONTRIBUTED AMOUNTS THAT
WOULD BE EXCESSIVE IF GIVEN TO A
CANDIDATE
67. Jonathan Krasno is a Professor of
Political Science at Binghamton University who
has authored an expert report in this litigation .
(Expert Report of Jonathan Krasno in NRSC v.
FEC, Unlimited Party Coordinated Expenditures
and Quid Pro Quo Corruption (“Krasno Rept.”), at
1, FEC Exh. 1 (Doc. 36-1, PageID 397).)  Professor
Krasno has published numerous works in the field
of political science, many of which involve the role

407

of campaign finance regulation and political
parties in United States politics . (Id. at
Curriculum Vitae 1-4, PageID 416-421). Professor
Krasno also co -wrote an expert report that was
explicitly relied upon by the Supreme Court in
FEC v. Colorado Republican Federal Campaign
Committee, 533 U.S. 431, 470 (2001) (“Colorado II”)
(citing Expert Report of Frank J. Sorauf &
Jonathan S. Krasno in Colorado II , Political
Parties and Coordinated Spending, FEC Exh. 2
(Doc. 36-2, PageID 423 - 474)). Professor Krasno’s
expert report, Political Party Committees and
Coordinated Expenditures, was relied upon by
both the district and appellate courts in the Cao v.
FEC litigation. (FEC Exh. 3 (“Krasno Cao  Rept.”)
(Doc. 36-3, PageID 478- 511).)  See generally In re
Cao, 619 F.3d 410 (5th Cir. 2010) (“Cao II”); Cao v.
FEC, 688 F. Supp. 2d 498 (E.D. La. 2010) (“Cao I”).
68. As Professor Krasno has explained,
“[m]uch of the history of US parties has been tied
up in exactly the sort of quid pro quo corruption
scandals that Congress has hoped to  eliminate or
minimize with existing law.”  (Krasno Rept. at 10,
FEC Exh. 1 (Doc. 36-1, PageID 408).)
69. The Democratic National Committee
was first formed in 1848 for the purpose of
planning the party’s next nominating convention.
The Republicans formed their national committee
a decade later. And in the late 19th and early 20th
centuries, the Framers’ concerns about corruption

Party coordinated communications generally

coordinated with a candidate or campaign that
expressly advocates for the election or defeat of a
clearly identified federal candidate, or references a
federal candidate within a certain period of time
prior to a f ederal primary or general election . 11
CFR § 109.37(a).

A. Political Parties Enjoy Significant
Advantages in Raising and
Spending Money in Connection With
Federal Elections, Including Higher
Contribution Limits
251. According to Professor Krasno, “[n]o
one can look at how the national [legislative
campaign committees], definitely including the
NRSC and NRCC, have fared under the current
campaign finance law without concluding that they
have prospered beyond their  wildest dreams prior
to its passage.” (Krasno Rept. at 15, FEC Exh. 1
(Doc. 36-1 PageID 413); see also Krasno Cao Rept.
at 1, FEC Exh. 3 (Doc. 36-3, PageID 480) (Political
parties “have been strongly advantaged by the
system of financing campaigns.”).)
252. There are three types of national
political party committees: national committees,
House campaign committees, and Senate
campaign committees. 11 C.F.R. § 110.1(c)(2); see
also 52 U.S.C. § 30101(14) (defining “national
committee”), (16) (defining “political party”). As
with other political parties, the Republican Party
maintains multiple national party committees: the
Republican National Committee (“RNC”), the

503

National Republican Congressional Committee
(“NRCC”), and the National Republican Senatorial
Committee (“NRSC”). (Clark Decl. ¶  3, FEC Exh.
13 (Doc. 36-13, PageID 1284).) The national party
committees for the Democratic Party are: the
Democratic National Committee (“DNC”), the
Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee
(“DCCC”), and the Democratic Senatorial
Campaign Committee (“DSCC”). (Id.)
253. A party’s national committee, Senate
campaign committee, and House campaign
committee are each considered separate national
party committees with separate contribution
limits. 11 C.F.R. § 110.1(c)(2)-(3).
254. As of January 1, 2023, the inflation -
adjusted limit for contributions from an individual
to a national party committee’s general account is
$41,300 per calendar year. 52  U.S.C.
§ 30116(a)(1)(B); FEC, Price Index Adjustments for
Contribution and Expenditure Limitations and
Lobbyist Bundling Disclosure Threshold, 88 Fed.
Reg. 7088, 7090 (Feb. 2,  2023) (“2023 Inflation
Index”).
255. In addition, as of January 1, 2023,
individuals may also give up to $123,900 per
calendar year to each of a national party
committee’s separate, segregated accounts for: (i)
election recounts and contests and other legal
proceedings; and (ii) national  party headquarters
buildings. 52 U.S.C. § 30116(a)(9); 2023 Inflation
Index, 88 Fed. Reg. at 7090. NRSC and NRCC have
both such accounts. (Declaration of Jason
Thielman (“Thielman Decl.”) ¶  4 (Doc. 19 -1,

504

PageID 175); Declaration of Chris Winkelman
(“Winkelman Decl.”) ¶ 4 (Doc. 19-2, PageID 185).)
Individuals may give an additional $123,900 per
calendar year to the party’s national committee’s
(but not the parties’ national congressional
campaign committees) separate, segregated
account for its presidential nominating convention.
52 U.S.C. § 30116(a)(9); 2023 Inflation Index, 88
Fed. Reg. at 7090. The spending of funds from
these separate, segregated accounts may be done
in coordination with candidates since  they are
exempted from the definition of coordinated party
expenditure under 52 U.S.C. § 30116(d)(5).
256. By contrast, when nonconnected
political committees make contributions to
candidates and candidate committees, they may do
so only with funds that have been received up to
$5,000 per year from an individual donor for such
purpose. 52 U.S.C. § 30116(a)(1)(C). And, as of
November 9, 2022, the inflation -adjusted limit for
contributions from an individual to a candidate is
$3,300 per election, with primary and general
elections being treated as separate elections. 52
U.S.C. § § 30116(a)(1)(A), (a)(6); 2023 Inflation
Index, 88 Fed. Reg. at 7090.
257. Under the Act, national party
committees can receive up to $15,000 per year from
other multicandidate political committees for their
general account and $45,000 for each of their
separated, segregated accounts per year. 52 U.S.C.
§ 30116(a)(2)(B). For accounts that make
contributions or coordinated expenditures,
multicandidate political committees can
themselves receive only $5,000 per year from

505

individuals or other multicandidate political
committees. 52  U.S.C. § 30116(a)(1)(C), (2)(C).
Candidates can receive only $5,000 per election
from a multicandidate political committee. 52
U.S.C. § 30116(a)(2).
258. An individual who desires to support
a political party may not only contribute to the
party’s national committees, but also to its state,
district, and local committees up to a combined
$10,000 per year. 52 U.S.C. § 30116(a)(1)(D). The
limit is shared between a state party and
“affiliated” local committees, but local committees
of a given political party may receive separate
contributions of up to $5,000 per year from
individuals if the committee’s fundraising is
generally separate from — and thus the committee
is not “affiliated” with — the state committee of
their political party. See, e.g., FEC Advisory Op.
2005-02 (Corzine), at 6- 7 ,
http://saos.fec.gov/aodocs/2005-02.pdf.
259. A party’s state, district, and local
committees can also receive what are known as
“Levin Funds,” named after the sponsor of the
relevant amendment. 52 U.S.C. § 30125(b); 11
C.F.R. §§ 300.2(h), 300.30-32. These are donations
of up to $10,000 per year per donor, and they may
come from sources ordinarily impermissible under
the Act, such as corporations or labor unions. 52
U.S.C. § 30125(b)(2)(B)(iii); 11 C.F.R. § 300.31(c).
The $10,000 Levin funds limit is separate from
FECA’s $10,000 limit on contribut ions from
individuals to state and local committees, and it is
reduced if state law establishes a lower limit. 11
C.F.R. § 300.31(d). Levin  funds can be used in

506

conjunction with hard money1 for certain activities
that benefit federal candidates, such as generic
party voter registration drives, voter identification
programs, and get - out-the-vote efforts. 52 U.S.C.
§ 30125(b)(2)(A); 11 C.F.R. § 300.32; see also
McConnell, 540 U.S. at 162- 63. The FEC’s
guidebook Political Party Committees (Aug. 2013),
http://www.fec.gov/pdf/partygui.pdf, provides a
summary of how Levin funds may be raised, spent,
and allocated. Id. at 57-58 (raising and spending);
Id. at 116-17 (allocation).
260. According to FEC records, between
January 1, 2009 through December 31, 2022,
Republican and Democratic state and local party
committees registered with the Commission have
received a total of $42,636,070 in Levin funds
receipts and made a combined total of $43,380,090
in Levin funds disbursements. (Clark Decl. ¶ 23,
FEC Exh. 13 (Doc. 36-13, PageID 1306).)
261. A national party committee can
receive unlimited amounts as transfers from other
national party committees ( e.g., the RNC can
transfer unlimited amounts to the NRCC and vice
versa). 52 U.S.C. § 30116(a)(4). A national party
committee can also receive unlimited amounts of
hard money as transfers from state, district, and
local party committees, and vice versa. 52  U.S.C.
§§ 30116(a)(4), 30125(a)(1). State, district, and
local party committees can also transfer hard


1 “Hard money” is a term of art referring to funds from
contributions that have been raised pursuant to FECA’s

507

money to one another without limit under the Act.
52 U.S.C. § 30116(a)(4). And candidate campaigns
can transfer funds to national, state, or local
committees of political parties “without
limitation.” 52 U.S.C. § 30114(a)(4).
262. The Act provides special exemptions
to the definitions of contributions and
expenditures for parties, which means some party
activities are not subject to any contribution limit.
Payment of compensation for legal or accounting
services by full-time staff on behalf of any political
party committee or candidate is excluded from
these definitions. 52 U.S.C.  § 30101(8)(B)(viii)(I),
(9)(B)(vii). The Act also excludes, for parties and
candidates, the use of real or personal property,
such as a community room , and the costs of
invitations, food, and beverages voluntarily
provided by an individual to any political
committee, provided that the value of an
individual’s activity does not exceed $1,000 for a
candidate per election and $2,000 for a political
party per year. 52 U.S.C. § 30101(8)(B)(ii). The Act
excludes from the definition of contribution for
parties and candidates the payment of travel
expenses incurred by any individual on behalf of
the candidate or party, as long as the cumulative
value of the expenses incurred by an individual
does not exceed $1,000 for a candidate per election
and $2,000 for a political party per year. 52 U.S.C.
§ 30101 (8)(B)(iv)). State and local parties may pay
for the costs of some communications, such as slate
cards, sample ballots, or other materials
distributed by volunteers, without regard to the
contribution and expenditure limits, even if those

508

activities are coordinated with candidates. 52
U.S.C. § 301018(B)(v), (9)(B)(iv); FEC,
Coordinated and Independent Expenditures, 68
Fed. Reg. 421, 449 (Jan. 3, 2003). The Act also
excludes, for state and local parties, expenditures
for certain campaign materials, as well as certain
voter registration and get -out-the-vote activities.
52 U.S.C. § 30101(9)(B)(viii)-(ix). Certain transfers
of payments received by political party committees
as a condition of ballot access are also excluded
from the definition of  “expenditure.” 52 U.S.C.
§ 30101(9)(B)(x).
263. Political parties also receive special
non-monetary benefits in connection with federal
elections. Unlike interest groups, parties have
their names next to those of their candidates on
ballots in most states. Major -party nominees are
automatically inc luded on the general election
ballot, and the names or symbols of their parties
are printed near their names. States also often run
parties’ primary elections. Krasno and Sorauf
McConnell Report at 25, FEC Exh. 4 (Doc. 36- 4,
PageID 537); see also  Rufer Certification Order
¶ 39 , FEC Exh. 7 (Doc. 36-7, PageID 972).
264. Unlike political parties, “[o]ther
entities are not entitled to organize the slate of
candidates presented to voters. Other entities do
not organize legislative caucuses, assign
committee chairs and members, or elect legislative
leadership…. Even the largest political action
committees cannot begin to approach the political
scope, influence, or depth of electoral support
characteristic of the Republican or Democratic

509

Parties.” (D. Green McConnell  Rebuttal Report at
8, FEC Exh. 5 (Doc. 36-5, PageID 655).)
265. Political parties also receive favorable
treatment in the amounts that they can contribute
to federal campaigns, including the amounts that
they can spend in coordination with their
candidates. 52 U.S.C. § 30116(d), (h). For example,
as of January 1, 2023, a party’s national committee
and its Senatorial campaign committee may
contribute another $57,800 combined per
campaign to each Senate candidate, which is in
addition to the $5,000 in contributions that al l
multicandidate political committees can mak e
under 52 U.S.C. § 30116(a)(2). 52 U.S.C.
§ 30116(h); 2023 Inflation Index, 88 Fed. Reg. at
7090.
266. The Act’s contribution limits apply
both to direct contributions of money and in - kind
contributions of goods or services. 52 U.S.C.
§ 30101(8)(A); 11 C.F.R. § 100.52. Generally,
expenditures made in coordination with a
candidate or their campaign are considered in-kind
contributions to the candidate and therefore the
Act’s contribution limits apply both to direct
contributions of money and in- kind contributions
of goods or services. 52 U.S.C. §§ 30101(8)(A),
30116(a)(7)(B); 11 C.F.R. § 100.52. However, there
is a special exception for “coordinated party
expenditures,” which are a special type of
expenditure that can be made only by a national or
state political party committee in connection with
the general election of a candidate. 11 C.F.R.
§§ 109.30-109. 37.

510

267. These party coordinated expenditures
are subject to a separate set of limits and do not
count against the party’s normal contribution
limits with respect to each candidate. 11  C.F.R.
§ 109.32(a)(3)(ii), 109.32(b)(4). Accordingly, party
committees are entitled to spend substantially
more money in coordinated support of their
candidates for federal office than other political
groups. National party committees can make
substantial coordinat ed party expenditures on
behalf of House, Senate, and presidential
nominees. State party committees may also spend
substantial amounts on coordinated party
expenditures to support their U.S. House and

entity is permitted to make these coordinated
expenditures under the Act, which are in addition
to the $5,000 in contributions that all
multicandidate political committees can make
under 52 U.S.C. § 30116(a)(2).

a political party’s national and state committees

coordinate spending with a House of
Representatives candidate up to $59,400 in states
with more than one congressi onal district and
$118,700 in states with only one congressional
district; and a Senate candidate in a range from

U.S.C. § 30116(d)(3); 2023 Inflation Index, 88 Fed.

511

planning the party’s next nominating convention.
The Republicans formed their national committee
a decade later. The goal of the RNC then was

Exh. 3 (Doc. 36 -3, PageID 501).) The ability of a
political party to influence elections can be judged

they have been for much of their history. “Political
scientists generally describe parties as having
three manifestations or guises: in the electorate
(i.e. party identification), in government (e.g. party
caucuses in legislatures) and as organizations.

1. Political Parties Can and Do

290. Under the Act, individuals, political
parties, and other political committees are all
limited in the amounts that they can contribute to
one candidate in a given election cycle. 52 U.S.C.
§ 30116(a)(1).
291. Under the current limits, a federal
candidate is limited to $6,600 in contributions from
each individual and non- multicandidate political
action committee in a given election cycle ($3,300
in a primary election and an additional $3,300 in
the general election). 52 U.S.C. § 30116(a)(1)(A),
(a)(6); 2023 Inflation Index, 88 Fed. Reg. at 7090.
292. National, state, local, and district
party committees are considered multicandidate
political committees under the Act, and therefore
each is generally limited to $10,000 in
contributions to one candidate in a given election
cycle ($5,000 in the prima ry and $5,000 in the
general election). 52 U.S.C. §§  30101(4), (16),
30116(a)(2)(A), (a)(4). A party’s national committee
and its Senatorial campaign committee, however,
may contribute up to $57,800 combined to each
Senate candidate in the 2024 election cy cle. 52
U.S.C. § 30116(h); 2023 Inflation Index, 88 Fed.
Reg. at 7090.
293. Candidates can receive contributions

committees, as well as state and local committees

3. Political Parties Can Legally
Engage in Numerous Activities
That Benefit Candidates,
Including Independent
Expenditures and Coordinated
Communications Made Prior to
the Few Months Before an
Election
307. Coordinated expenditures are those
that are made in “cooperation, consultation or
concert with, or at the request or suggestion of” the
candidate or candidate’s authorized committee. 11
C.F.R. § 109.20; see also  52 U.S.C. § 30101(17)
(defining “independent expenditure”).
Expenditures made by political parties that are not
coordinated with a candidate are considered
independent expenditures. 52 U.S.C. 30101(17).
308. Generally, political parties may make
unlimited independent expenditures . Colorado II,
533 U.S. at 465; Colorado I, 518 U.S. at 618. Party
independent expenditures are limited only where
the national committee of a political party has been
designated as the  authorized committee of a
Presidential candidate and the campaign is subject
to public financing restrictions. 11 C.F.R.
§§ 109.36, 9002.1.
309. Party coordinated communications
are one category of coordinated expenditures that
are limited under the Act. 11 C.F.R. § 109.37. Just

529

like other expenditures, party communications
that are not coordinated with federal candidates or
their campaigns are considered independent and
parties may generally engage in them without
limit. Colorado II, 533 U.S. at 465; Colorado I, 518
U.S. at 618.
310. Not every communication is
considered a party coordinated communication
even if it there is some level of communication with
the candidate or candidate’s authorized committee.
Under the Commission’s regulations, whether a
particular communication is considered to be a
party coordinated communication is based upon
both the conduct of those involved and the content
of the communication. 11 C.F.R. § 109.37.
311. Prior to 90 days before a
Congressional or Senate election, or 120 days
before a Presidential election, a party
communication is not deemed coordinated with a
candidate unless it “disseminates, distributes, or
republishes . . . campaign materials prepared by a
candidate, …” or “expressly advocates the election
or defeat of a clearly identified candidate.” 11
C.F.R. § 109.37(a)(2)(i)-(ii). No other party
communications made prior to the 90/120 day
windows count against the Act’s limits on party
contributions or party coordinated expenditures.
312. Even within the 90 or 120 days
immediately before an election, a party
communication is not considered a party
coordinated communication subject to the Act’s
limits unless it refers to a clearly identified federal
candidate and is disseminated within that

530

candidate’s jurisdiction. 11 C.F.R.
§ 109.37(a)(2)(iii).
313. A party communication also is not
considered coordinated unless the party and
candidate have engaged in specific conduct
indicating coordination, even if the communication
is disseminated within 90 or 120 days before an
election and refers to a clearl y identified federal
candidate in the appropriate jurisdiction. 11 C.F.R.
§ 109.37(a)(3); see also  id. § 109.21(d)(1)-(6). The
conduct standard is met if, e.g. , “[t]he
communication is created, produced, or distributed
at the request or suggestion of a can didate,” “[t]he
communication is created, produced, or distributed
after one or more substantial discussions about the
communication between the person paying for the
communication . . . and the candidate who is
clearly identified in the communication,” or  the
person paying for the communication hires a
candidate’s vendor or former employee “to create,
produce, or distribute” it and in doing so that
vendor/employee uses “material” information
about “campaign plans, projects, activities, or
needs” or shares such information with the payer.
11 C.F.R. § 109.21(d)(1)(i), (d)(3), (d)(4)-(5).
314. A party can avoid having a
communication deemed a coordinated
communication by setting up and distributing a
written “firewall” policy that prohibits the flow of
information between the individuals “providing
services for the [party] paying for the
communication” and the individuals who are
“currently or [were] previously providing services
to the candidate who is clearly identified in the

531

communication [or his or his opponent’s
committee].” 11 C.F.R. § 109.21(h); see also  id.
§ 109.37(a)(3).
315. In practice, the RNC has decided to
create its “firewall” by approving a budget for
independent expenditures, and then supplying
that budget to individual consulting groups that
“have no connection, no ability to deal with
campaigns.” (RNC 30(b)(6) Cao Dep. at 58:22- 59:8,
FEC Exh. 8 (Doc. 36 -8, PageID 944 -45).) The
consultant then creates and runs  advertising,
without any input or control from the RNC or its
officers. (Id. at59:4-60:5 (Doc. 36 - 8, PageID 945 -
46).)
4. Outside the Highly
Consequential Prioritized Races,
the Effects of the Coordinated
Limits Are Very Modest
316. “Parties want winners – to solidify
their grip on power, to expand their presence
across the nation, to satisfy their supporters, etc. –
so they look for races where their involvement
could mean the difference between victory and
defeat.” (Krasno Cao Rept. at 19, FEC Exh. 3 (Doc.
36-3, PageID 498).)
317. Political parties “try to maximize
their impact by working hardest in – or targeting –
the races they deem closest.” (Krasno Cao Rept. at
19, FEC Exh. 3 (Doc. 36 -3, PageID 498).) As a
result, candidates that are viewed as “safe
incumbents” or “hopeless” are typically ignored by
party committees. (Id.) Parties “try to spend less on

532

uncompetitive races in order to spend more on
competitive ones.” (Id.)
318. Political parties “allocate[ ] money
based on a number of factors, including ‘the
financial strength of the campaign,’ ‘what [the
candidate’s] poll numbers looked like,’ and ‘who
had the best chance of winning or who needed the
money most.’” Colorado II , 533 U.S. at 478
(quoting, inter alia, Decl. of Robert Hickmott in
Colorado II , former Democratic fundraiser and
National Finance Director for Timothy Wirth’s
Senate campaign, FEC Exh.11 (Doc. 36-11, PageID
1182, 1183)); see also Decl. of Robert Hickmot t in
McConnell ¶ 4 (reaffirming declaration in
Colorado II ), FEC Exh. 12 (Doc. 36 -12, PageID
1276)). “[T]he primary consideration in allocating
funds is which races are marginal — that is, which
races are ones where party money could be the
difference between winning and losing . . . .” FEC
v. Colorado Republican Fed. Campaign Comm., 41
F. Supp. 2d 1197, 1203 (D. Colo. 1999), aff’d , 213
F.3d 1221 (10th Cir. 2000), rev’d on other grounds,
533 U.S. 431, 121 S. Ct. 2351 (2001); see also supra
Section IV.B.
319. As a result of their focus on close
races, party committees rarely reach their legal
limit for coordinated expenditures in a particular
House or Senate race. There are 435 seats in the
U.S. House of Representatives, each of which is
filled by an election during every two-year election
cycle. U.S. Const. art. I, § 2, cl. 1. There are 100
seats in the U.S. Senate, and one third of the total
Senate membership is elected every two- year
election cycle. U.S. Const. art. I, § 3, cl. 1. Although

533

there are at least 468 federal elections each cycle,
Republican committees reached the maximum
amount of coordinated expenditures in only eight
congressional races in 2022 and five races in 2020.
(Clark Decl. ¶ 9, Tables 11 & 12, FEC Exh. 13 (Doc.
36-13, PageID 1291- 92).) Democratic committees
only reached the legal limit in six congressional
races in 2022 and six races in 2020. (Id.)
320. In only a small fraction of races do
party committees spend 95% or more of the
coordinated expenditures available to them under
the Act. Republican committees only reached the
95% threshold in coordinated expenditures in 74
congressional races (15%) i n 2022, and in 36 (8%)
in 2020. (Clark Decl. ¶ 9, Tables 11 & 12, FEC Exh.
13 (Doc. 36- 13, PageID 1291-  92).) Democratic
committees only reached the 95% standard in five

334. When enacting FECA, Congress also
amended section 315 of the Communications Act of
1934 to provide that, during the 45 days preceding
a primary, caucus, or runoff election, and during
the 60 days preceding a general or special election,
broadcasters must charge candidates for their
campaign advertisements at the same rate that the
broadcaster offers their most favored commercial
customer for the same class, amount, and time
period ( e.g., if their most favored commercial
customer is offered a volume discount, the
candidate gets the benefit of that volume discount
even if the candidate does not buy in volume).
Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971, Pub. L.
No. 92 –225, § 103(a)(1), 86 Stat. 3, 4 (1972)
(codified as amended at 47 U.S.C. § 315(b)(1)(A));
47 CFR § 73.1942(a)(1); FCC, The L. of Pol. Broad.
& Cablecasting, 69 F.C.C.2d 2209, 2220- 21, 2273,
2276-77 (1978). At all other times, broadcasters
must charge candidates at the same rate for
comparable use of the station by commercial

541

advertisers. 47 U.S.C. § 315(b)(1)(B); 47 C.F.R.
§ 73.1942(a)(2).
335. NRSC and NRCC’s claim that their
failure to obtain the lowest unit charge during cost
them “millions of dollars in added fees for
purchased advertising time,” (NRSC Discovery
Responses, Resp. to Interr. 7, FEC Exh. 10 (Doc.
36-10, PageID 1148); NRCC D iscovery Responses,
Resp. to Interr. 7, FEC Exh. 9 (Doc. 36 -9, PageID
1092)), is wholly unsubstantiated by documentary
evidence and thus cannot be countenanced.
336. Moreover, Congress intended the
“lowest unit charge” provision to facilitate access
by political candidates “to the broadcast media to
explain their stand on issues and to limit the cost
of campaigning for public office.” KVUE, Inc. v.
Moore, 709 F.2d 922 (5th Cir. 1983), aff’d sub nom.
Texas v. KVUE-TV, Inc., 465 U.S. 1092 (1984). At
the same time, however, Congress sought to ensure
that any attempt to “lower the rates charged
candidates” should avoid “imposing unreasonable
and possibly economically d evastating burdens on
small stations.” Hernstadt v. FCC , 677 F.2d 893,
898 (D.C. Cir. 1980); see also id. at 898 n.15 (citing
S. Rep.  92-96, 92d Cong., 1st Sess. 27 (1971));
KVUE, Inc. , 709 F.2d at 936 & n.64; Federal
Election Campaign Act of 1971: Hearings on S. 1,
et al., Before the Subcomm. on Communications of
the Senate Comm. on Commerce, 92d Cong., 1st
Sess. 412 (1971) (Sen. Pastore).
337. To facilitate candidate access to
broadcast stations without either causing undue
financial hardship to licensees or discouraging

542

them from offering to sell time for political
discussion, Congress has “carefully circumscribed”
the federal requirement for charging “lowest unit
charge” rates. KVUE, Inc., 709 F.2d at 936. Among
other things, Congress chose to limit the lowest
unit charge provision to “legally qualified
candidates” and did not include political party
committees. Id. at 935 -36, 936 n.63; see also  47
U.S.C. § 315(b)(1); FCC, Use of Broadcast &
Cablecast Facilities by Candidates for Public
Office, 34 F.C.C. 2d 510, 529 (1972) (explaining
that the lowest unit charge provision does not
apply to broadcasts by “groups, organizations or
persons other than candidates”).
338. Federally mandating broadcasters to
give party committees the lowest unit charge for an
unlimited number of party coordinated
communications as plaintiffs demand, ( see Compl.
¶¶ 33, 39 (Doc. 1, PageID 9, 10 -11); Pls. Proposed
Facts ¶ 39 (Doc. 21 -1, PageID 269),) would
frustrate this “carefully circumscribed” federal
plan.
339. Indeed, Congress rejected a proposal
that, inter alia , would have expanded the
application of the lowest unit charge provision visa-vis party committees even when party
coordinated communications were to be limited.
The Senate version of the Bipartisan Campaign
Reform Act included the “Torricelli Amendment, ”
which would have, inter alia, expanded the
availability of the lowest unit rate provision vis -avis party committees. Congressional Record —
Senate S2567 (Mar. 20, 2001), S2618 (Mar. 21,
2001). There was an entire hearing before a House

543

of Representative’s subcommittee regarding this
amendment during which several members
expressed their concern about the deleterious
impacts of the Torricelli Amendment, such as the
increased burden on broadcasters. E.g., Hearing
Before House of Representative, Committee on
Energy and Commerce, Subcommittee on
Telecommunications and the Internet, Campaign
Finance Reform: Proposals Impacting
Broadcasters, Cable Operators and Satellite
Providers, 107th Cong., Serial No. 107-42 (June 20,
2001), at 2 (Chairman Fred Upton stating that the
Torricelli Amendment would “unfairly burden
broadcasters, cable operators and satellite
providers”); Id. at 5 (Vice Chairman Cliff Stearns);
id. at 8 (Rep. Lee Terry); see also  id. at 17, 18
(statement of Jack Sander, Executive Vice
President Media Operations, Belo Corp.). Members
also expressed concern that the amendment would
“seriously threaten the ability of State and local
candidates . . . to get on the air at all, since Federal
candidates for elected office are afforded
reasonable access to the airwaves, but State and
local candidates are not . . . [and] [i]n many
markets, there may be little or no advertising
inventory available for these races.” Id.  at 6 (Rep.
John D. Dingell); see also id. at 4-5 (Vice Chairman
Stearns discussing article about television stations
refusing to take ads from non -federal campaigns);
id. at 9 (Rep. Gene Green); cf.  id. at 14- 21
(statement of Jack Sander, Executive Vice
President Media Operations, Belo Corp.). Although
